Title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
Context: What can we learn from this Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk...
Full Text:
php2shell raised fears of mass exploitation. A week of testing by our research team found that working exploits had to be fitted to each target’s exact PHP setup. Systems that share one build, such as network appliances, are the exception: one tuned exploit can reach every device that runs it.

Key takeaways

The five vulnerable PHP sites we exposed to the internet were not compromised, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) that go beyond version checks do not reliably confirm whether a host is vulnerable. Exploitation has been confirmed elsewhere, on researcher honeypots and on some network appliances.

In realistic environments, turning php2shell into remote code execution usually takes an exploit built for the specific target. That is hard, not impossible, and it puts php2shell in a different category from Log4Shell, even though both received near-maximum severity ratings. Where many systems share one build, such as network appliances, a single calibrated exploit can work against all of them.

Patch now, starting with internet-facing management interfaces, network appliances, and end-of-life PHP branches. Tenable Nessus and Tenable One Web App Scanning have had version-based detection since October 21.

Background

On October 20, 2026, PHP announced two vulnerabilities, and on October 21 released fixes for flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Each has a CVSSv4 score of 9.2. For a full breakdown of affected versions, fixes and mitigations, see our frequently asked questions blog post.

This post covers what happened after the disclosure, based on what our team observed directly.

From disclosure to headline in under 48 hours

php2shell got big fast. Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online before the official release. Within two days, the vulnerability had a name, a logo and coverage in mainstream media.

Several websites went offline as a precaution, as described in our threat actor response blog post. Censys’s php2shell dashboard, which tracks PHP services by reported version, showed about 30.3 million PHP services still on an affected version on October 29, though a matching version does not mean a system can be exploited.

The comparison with Log4Shell came up early, but the two are very different to exploit. With Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), attackers only had to send a short piece of text to a vulnerable application, for example in a login form or a web request. If the application logged that text, the attack worked. The same text worked against almost any vulnerable target without changes, so attackers could launch it at scale within hours, and many of those attacks succeeded.

php2shell is different. Exploitation depends on the state of the heap, the process manager in use, worker reuse and how memory is laid out on a given build. php2shell drew attention quickly, but attackers can't exploit it as easily as Log4Shell.

What changed while we were testing

Several developments that matter for defenders came after our research began:

On October 24, honeypots run by Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three sensors running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, a configuration that favors the exploit.

On October 26, CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Federal civilian agencies have until October 29 to remediate.

The same day, security firm Dream reported an attack chain that combined php2shell with a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw, Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300). Dream says the campaign rooted “25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.” Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 says it independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results. We have not verified these findings ourselves.

On October 28, CISA added Fragnesia to the KEV catalog and noted that it can be chained with php2shell to run commands as root. By October 29, Palo Alto Networks reported active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces.

These reports are consistent with what we found. The exploit has to be calibrated to a specific build. Network appliances often run the same software across many devices, so one calibrated exploit can reach many of them. That is where we expect targeted exploitation to keep growing.

What we observed during our exploit research

Exposed targets

To measure real-world activity, we kept five vulnerable PHP sites reachable from the internet: four through the evening of October 24, and one still running in a standard, vulnerable configuration at the time of writing.

Over that period, we observed mass exploitation attempts that matched php2shell exploitation patterns. None of our targets had been compromised as of October 29.

Other organizations have reported exploitation attempts and, in the cases described above, successful exploitation. Amazon Threat Intelligence says php2shell is “now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.” Our data does not contradict these reports. It shows that attempts, even at scale, were not enough to compromise a default installation in our environment. Attempts and successful compromises are two different numbers, and in the first days after a disclosure people often treat them as the same.

Public proofs-of-concept

We collected and tested almost all public PoCs. An early lead was php2shell poc, published by researcher Daniel Púa (devploit). It let us reproduce the exposure on multiple 8.4 and 8.5 environments with specific configurations. From there, we did deeper research, including white-box testing and code and patch comparison, and achieved remote code execution on PHP 7.4.33.

What we learned from this research is that the exploit inadvertently reveals a clean discriminator: the same multipart POST that begins stage 1 produces a different allocator response on patched vs. unpatched PHP. No heap corruption, no crash, no shell, just a measurable size difference in how the server handles the request. That became signal 1: a large filename in the multipart request produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable versions than on fixed versions, because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Same request, same PHP – different memory behavior depending solely on whether the UAF patch is present.

Tenable Research identified a second signal as well: the compact amplification sequences that exercise the UAF window's existence without triggering corruption. The session upload-progress oracle watches for the crash/recover pattern that vulnerable versions exhibit under controlled amplification.

These two signals became a stateful probe that a Nessus ‘direct check’ plugin could detect. However, the probe would miss some vulnerable systems and flag some patched ones as vulnerable.

The memory corruption is real, and PHP confirms memory disclosure as one of the impacts. Turning it into code execution on a target is difficult and unique to each target. Our working RCE required an exploit tuned to the target's environment, including its PHP build, SAPI, extensions and runtime configuration. A payload that works against one lab setup does not carry over to a different distribution package or a different PHP-FPM pool configuration.

AI-accelerated research: Useful, but it needs checking

AI agents sped up our reverse engineering and testing, and they also produced at least one convincing false positive. During a multi-hour session, an agent built a working shell against our PHP-FPM lab containers and reported it as confirmation of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. It was not. The agent had used a local file inclusion weakness that we had added to the lab, a different attack class that does not exist in default PHP deployments. A researcher caught the error by checking the exploit chain against the vulnerability's mechanics.

The lesson applies to anyone reading exploitation claims this week: a real shell is not proof that a specific CVE was used. We also ran into inconsistent responses from AI tools when doing authorized exploit validation, which slowed parts of the work.

White-box testing

The GDB analysis and heap geometry research below show why: there is no universal offset. Code execution is a real exposure yet it is not as simple as portrayed. The RCE we achieved on PHP 7.4.33 worked only once the exploit matched that one setup. A profile that achieves a shell against one lab container does not carry over to a different distribution package, a different PHP-FPM pool configuration, or a different memory limit.

The chunk-relative offsets pictured in the ‘heap geometry capture method’ visuals below reference _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0, arData at chunk+0x64b80. These values illustrate the measurement method and are specific to PHP 8.3.35 built from the docker-library bookworm image on amd64. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or a PHP 8.3.35 built with different extensions, produces different chunk geometry values. We used GDB against the live worker to measure the actual values for a given target.

Our failure to show that mass exploitation is quick or easy does not make this vulnerability harmless. A well-resourced attacker who wants a specific target can build that exploit, and AI-assisted tooling shortens the time it takes. It does make mass exploitation of the Log4Shell kind much less likely. The exception is any population of systems that share one build, such as network appliances, where the cost of calibration is paid once.

Why exploitation is hard

When possible, Tenable Research releases exposure direct checks to help customers detect exploitable vulnerabilities within their environments. These direct checks depend on finding reliable and safe methods of exercising a vulnerability in a way that simulates an exploit without triggering any destructive actions. This typically involves first researching how to develop an exploit, then figuring out how to test that safely.

Our research found the php2shell exposure difficult to reproduce broadly, even with white-box testing and GDB attached to processes, and even with AI agents analyzing runtime memory and source code for weaknesses and leads in parallel. What we learned from this research helps to inform us on the practical realities of real-world exploitation:

php2shell is a multi-stage memory corruption chain. A direct check triggering an out-of-memory condition alone does not fully guarantee the asset is also exposed to remote code execution.

In-memory offsets are version and system specific. The chunk-relative structure offsets required for heap manipulation change with every PHP patch release and system/software combination. Gaps in an inventory of known offsets and platforms could make a vulnerable system look patched (false-negative).

The OOM trigger depends on application-controlled memory limits. Whether the condition fires depends on the configured memory_limit and on whether the application overrides it via ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives.

The use-after-free requires reuse of the PHP worker across consecutive requests. Under mod_php, keep-alive pins a connection to one worker; under FPM, session affinity (PHPSESSID) is required. Both depend on SAPI and process-manager settings. For example, pm.max_requests recycles workers and breaks the use-after-free chain with no visible sign, so the check returns a false negative.

The exploit crashes PHP workers. Workers appear to respawn reliably, but a direct check that intentionally degrades performance could still affect production systems.

What can we learn from this

Inevitably, when a remote code execution vulnerability is discovered in a broadly deployed core component of the services we use, a knee-jerk reaction is triggered that creates significant fears of mass exploitation and extreme risk. While we do not want to downplay the dangers of this vulnerability, it is valuable to understand the practicalities of exploitation in the real world versus the fear that is built around a CVE during the regular news cycle. In this case, that nuance points remediation first at internet-facing assets, especially appliances such as network infrastructure management interfaces, and anything else that runs a common, basic deployment that reduces overall complexity.

Prioritization matters more as AI finds more vulnerabilities

Calif, OpenAI and Wiz are credited with finding php2shell. Calif says AI assisted the discovery. We expect the number of disclosed vulnerabilities to keep rising as these tools improve, and many of them will come with high base scores. Patching everything rated critical at the speed of the news cycle will not be possible.

Security teams need to understand what a vulnerability takes to exploit, not only how bad the worst case is:

Is there a public exploit that works without changes, or only a crash PoC?

Does exploitation depend on a non-default configuration, a specific build or prior access?

Is the vulnerable component reachable from the internet in your environment?

Has anyone observed successful compromise, as opposed to scanning?

Exploit prediction scores such as EPSS, Tenable's Vulnerability Priority Rating (VPR) and confirmed exploitation sources such as CISA's KEV catalog help answer these questions. They work better alongside an analysis of the vulnerability itself than in place of one.

Patch anyway

Our observations do not mean php2shell should be ignored. The conditions for exploitation exist, exploit development will improve and targeted attacks against high-value PHP applications are plausible. Updating to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or applying your distribution's fixed packages, remains the recommendation. For end-of-life branches, plan an upgrade. Until then, apply the configuration mitigations described in our FAQ and limit internet exposure, starting with appliance management interfaces. For network appliances, PHP version numbers do not apply: use your vendor's fixed build or its interim mitigations.

What we are recommending is a different order of work. Patch or isolate internet-facing network appliances, management interfaces, and end-of-life PHP systems now. For the rest of your PHP estate, patch on your critical schedule, and check that less publicized vulnerabilities that are easy to exploit in your environment are not waiting behind php2shell.

Title: Whole-of-state defense: How SLED agencies can secure critical infrastructure in the AI era
Context: The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure,...
Full Text:
AI is widening the attack surface of the critical infrastructure facilities and services that state, local, and education (SLED) organizations run. In the final post of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we explain how a whole-of-state security approach can help SLED agencies protect their critical infrastructure.

Key takeaways

Because cyber attackers prey on under-resourced targets, they often go after SLED organizations, especially those that operate critical infrastructure, including water systems, hospitals, mass transit, emergency services, and schools.

In the latest research from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO), nearly 90% of state CIOs rated cyberattacks on critical systems as a high concern.

AI expands the attack surface in two fundamental ways: SLED agencies and employees adopt AI tools and AI-built apps faster than security teams can authorize and inventory them, while attackers use AI automation to find weak points faster.

A whole-of-state cybersecurity approach treats state agencies, counties, cities, school districts, and utilities as one defensive perimeter, with shared visibility, shared services, and clear governance.

Cyber attackers often look for the weakest link that can offer them an entry point into larger targets. If they can’t crack a state agency’s hardened systems, they’ll try to breach it in a roundabout way by first breaking into a small town’s water utility, a rural school district, or a county dispatch center, and then attempt to move laterally toward the bigger target.

When one of those weak links fails, the consequences can reach well beyond the breached agency: halted 911 dispatches, disrupted water service, exposed resident data, and more.

AI is further complicating the picture.

State, local, and education (SLED) organizations are adopting AI quickly to improve efficiency, employees are building applications with it informally, and adversaries are using it to speed up reconnaissance. Each of those developments is making it harder for security teams to protect SLED agencies.

In this fourth and final blog in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series, we focus on what that expanding AI attack surface means for state, local, and education cybersecurity leaders responsible for critical infrastructure, and how whole-of-state cybersecurity can help them stay ahead.

Why SLED critical infrastructure is a prime target

SLED organizations operate critical infrastructure, such as water treatment plants, transportation systems, public hospitals, schools, and emergency communications, across many of the 16 critical infrastructure sectors categorized by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

State technology leaders are concerned about protecting these critical infrastructure facilities and services from cyber attacks, as “The Expanding Cyber Perimeter” report, published in September by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO) and General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), found.

Here are five key findings from the report, which drew on the 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey, the 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte Cybersecurity Study, and interviews with state CISOs:

Nearly 90% of state CIOs rate cyber attacks on critical systems as a high concern. The rest rate them as moderate.

State CIOs report low confidence in local governments’ cyber practices. The report’s authors also say it’s unclear how states should help local governments and independent local government entities, like special districts.

Water and wastewater plants, dams, hospitals, and transportation services face the greatest cyber risk.

Many systems run on aging or proprietary operational technology (OT) with no upgrade path, and broad remote access increases their cyber risk.

Small communities and special districts often have limited cyber staff, aging equipment, and complex OT with few controls. With hundreds of such entities in a single state, attackers have plenty of entry points to try.

Responsibility is also murky. According to the NASCIO-GDIT report, it’s often unclear which agency is responsible for responding to an attack on critical infrastructure, especially where legal authority, governance, or partnerships aren’t in place.

Cyber risk extends beyond technical and geographical boundaries. When an attacker breaches systems of a county water utility or a school district, the incident can have widespread consequences.

State and local officials and their CIOs and CISOs should stop treating these incidents as one city’s or one county’s problem. Robert Beach, then CTO of the City of Cocoa, Florida, and a member of the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) executive committee, told StateScoop last year that an attack on critical infrastructure “is an attack on the nation.”

Insiders add another layer of risk. Another MS-ISAC report, “Strengthening Critical Infrastructure: SLTT Progress & Priorities,” published in August 2025, flagged excessive access to system controls as a vulnerability. The report recommended agencies review who can reach their networks and disable credentials promptly when employees leave.

The 2026 NASCIO-Deloitte study underscores the risk, noting that attackers exploit compromised credentials and former employee accounts, so regular access reviews and prompt offboarding remain essential.

Recent cyber attacks against water systems have made the threat very real. On July 30, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) warned that water and wastewater sector utilities in at least seven states had reported cyber attacks, leading in some cases to degraded water operations.

That same day, the CISA said it had observed “a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers” in the water and wastewater sector.

“Threat actors targeting exposed PLCs have modified passwords to lock out operators and disconnected the PLCs by changing their IP addresses. This activity has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” the CISA alert reads.

A week earlier, CISA and several federal agencies had published a joint advisory warning critical infrastructure organizations in the government, water, and energy sectors of “ongoing cyber exploitation of internet-connected OT devices.”

Tenable researchers recommend removing internet-exposed PLCs and setting their mode switches to “Run”, among other steps. The U.S. government is also tightening cybersecurity regulations for water and wastewater utilities.

Federal and state leaders are mobilizing, too.

In August, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, and Texas Cyber Command Chief Vice Admiral (Ret.) TJ White launched Project Watershed at a roundtable in San Antonio, Texas, which I was honored to attend. Project Watershed is a joint effort aimed at strengthening the cybersecurity of Texas water and wastewater systems against threats from hostile foreign adversaries.

Governor Abbott said that through the project, “our communities and water systems will be better secured from the onslaught of cyber-attacks.”

Protecting the water systems Americans rely on every day is a shared responsibility, and Project Watershed shows the kind of public-private collaboration a whole-of-state approach depends on.

How AI expands the attack surface

AI has moved from pilot project to operational reality in state government. NASCIO’s 2026 research shows AI overtaking cybersecurity as the top policy priority for state CIOs, the first time in more than a decade that cybersecurity loses the top spot.

AI adoption is good news for service delivery, but it also increases SLED agencies’ cyber risk. Three forces drive the rise in cyber risk:

Employees build and adopt AI tools on their own. As we covered earlier in this series, non-technical staff can now use AI tools to generate working applications using natural-language prompts, often without permission from the IT and security departments. In a government setting, those unsanctioned apps can access resident data, case management systems, and internal credentials, all without testing, patching, or monitoring.

AI shows up inside the software SLED agencies already own, as vendors quietly add AI features and connectors to their products, which can expand data access and permissions without the awareness of the IT and security teams.

Attackers use automation to move faster. The NASCIO-GDIT brief cites emerging threats such as automated reconnaissance, and it urges states to prepare for an increase in AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure, as the window between when an exposure appears and when attackers exploit it keeps shrinking.

For critical infrastructure operators, the stakes rise further. Their aging OT systems with broad remote access are already a soft target. Unvetted AI apps, over-permissioned connectors, and automated scanning by attackers quickly multiply the number of paths an attacker can chain together.

The key for SLED agency CISOs is to see their exposures across IT, OT, cloud, identity, and AI as one connected picture, and to prioritize and act on the ones an attacker could realistically exploit to reach systems that matter to public safety. An exposure management program can help SLED agencies address this cyber risk with comprehensive visibility, prioritization, and AI-assisted action.

What a whole-of-state approach looks like

A whole-of-state approach treats state agencies, local governments, schools, and utilities as one defensive perimeter instead of a collection of individual, siloed organizations.

The state government should share governance frameworks, visibility of IT/OT assets and security findings, and cybersecurity capabilities so the smallest entity doesn’t have to defend itself alone.

As Tenable’s Matt Kucik explains in the blog, “Whole-of-state cybersecurity: Uniting SLED agencies for maximum impact,” success starts with leadership and vision, open communication, and an actionable plan.

The model is gaining ground. The NASCIO-GDIT report found that 73% of states responding to the 2026 State CIO Survey include critical infrastructure cyber protection in their whole-of-state plans. It calls these models the main framework emerging for statewide resilience. Maturity varies widely, though. Four building blocks separate strong programs from weak ones:

Governance and clear roles. CISA’s state cybersecurity governance case studies highlight Georgia and Virginia, which use formal structures to treat cyber risk as a collective priority. They have proactively defined who is in charge of prevention, who is in charge of responding, and who is in charge of generating incident reports.

Shared visibility. You can’t prioritize what you can’t see. A statewide view of assets and exposures lets a small water district benefit from the same insight as a large state agency.

Shared services. In Utah, its federally funded shared services program offers endpoint protection, patching, training, and incident response to roughly 80% of local government entities in the state. The state secured an additional $1.5 million for water-sector cybersecurity.

Trust earned through results. What local partners need from the state is faster remediation, lower costs, and fewer surprises. New Jersey CISO Michael Geraghty made this point in the NASCIO-GDIT report: Telling local governments you’re from the state and here to help doesn’t earn their trust. Results do.

It’s also key to share information quickly. Terry Loftus, CIO of the San Diego County Office of Education and an MS-ISAC committee member, told StateScoop that many districts learn of attacks when they receive a ransomware demand.

State cybersecurity agencies should build channels that proactively push threat intelligence and exposure data to every entity in their state, to increase the chances of preventing attacks.

Five steps SLED agencies can take to boost their cyber defenses

Here’s Tenable’s advice on where to start, whether you lead a state agency, a county IT shop, a school district, or a municipal utility:

Create and continuously update a complete inventory of your critical infrastructure assets, including OT systems, remote access paths, and AI tools and apps. Start with the systems that affect public health and safety.

Prioritize by exploitability and impact. Don’t chase every finding. Focus on the exposures an attacker could realistically chain together to reach water, power, health, or emergency systems. Removing internet-exposed controllers and securing any remote access paths to them should be the highest priority.

Share visibility across jurisdictions. Give small entities access to the same insight larger agencies have, whether through statewide tooling, shared services, or regular information-sharing forums.

Govern AI use before it sprawls. Set clear policies, approved-tool lists, and training for employees who build with AI.

Check if State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP) funding is still available in your state to help fund these priorities.

How Tenable can help SLED agencies

Tenable One gives security teams unified visibility, insights and action across their organizations’ attack surface, including IT, cloud, identity, AI, and OT.

Tenable One OT Exposure capabilities extend that visibility, insight, and action to the OT and extended internet of things (xIoT) devices used by many critical infrastructure organizations.

With Tenable One, SLED teams can see what they have, understand which exposures matter most, and take prioritized actions, maximizing staff and grant dollars to drive down cyber risk.

The City of Raleigh in North Carolina, for example, uses Tenable to ensure the safety and sustainability of its public water systems. To see how Tenable supports statewide programs, explore our state, local, and education solutions and learn how Tenable helps meet SLCGP requirements.

Looking ahead

The attack surface is growing, a trend that AI is accelerating. Federal funding is shrinking, and its future is uncertain. Yet the fundamentals of resilience stay the same: know your assets, understand your exposures, share what you learn, and act together before an attacker forces your hand.

No single state or jurisdiction has solved this, and no single tool will. A whole-of-state approach gives SLED organizations the best chance to stay ahead of the threats facing the critical services residents rely on every day.

Respond faster with Tenable solutions

The recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have put security teams in a race against attackers to remediate or mitigate exposure before their systems are targeted. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, and many of those sites run unsupported, legacy branches that no longer receive upstream support. Organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

To help cybersecurity teams accelerate emergency response, this blog outlines tips for using the Tenable solutions to identify vulnerable versions of PHP, prioritize remediation decisions, and implement patches as quickly as possible.

External Attack Surface Management

Tenable One Attack Surface Management (ASM) helps you discover externally facing assets running PHP. ASM continuously scans public data sources, such as DNS records, IP addresses, Autonomous System Numbers (ASN), WHOIS registrations, and neighboring IP ranges, to discover forgotten, rogue, or shadow IT assets that might be vulnerable to PHP2Shell. This is one of the first steps to take. It shows your digital footprint from the attacker’s perspective and identifies potential entry points into your organization.

Important ASM tips include:

Use ASM to find additional top-level domains related to your organization. Suggested Domains helps you identify additional domains you may own based on ASN, brand, domain name, IP range, subdomain, or nameserver. You can also adjust the suggestion rules to prioritize domain names based on the likelihood of ownership.

Search the inventory for PHP deployments. Create a query in ASM to identify PHP as a programming language filter. This gives you a quick starting point to assess locations, asset details, and software versions for further analysis.

Continuously monitor for changes in your attack surface. Use Subscriptions in ASM to receive event-driven notifications and understand important changes in your attack surface that may create new exposure. Choose from hundreds of pre-built event categories or create a customized subscription. Two subscriptions apply to PHP: PHP in applications and PHP end-of-life installs.

Enabling thorough testing and paranoia mode in your scan policy conducts deeper assessments of your attack surface using multiple methods to discover risk. This is very important when you need to scan software across all system drives or investigate deep component-level software vulnerabilities where default settings may result in false negatives.

Title: The adversary economy: How threat actors are reacting to PHP2Shell
Context: They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation,...
Full Text:
Two critical PHP vulnerabilities sent criminal forum operators scrambling to protect their own infrastructure, revealing that threat actors face the same exposure management challenges as the organizations they target.

Key takeaways

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy.

Forum self-evacuations: Criminal forums including BreachForums initiated emergency infrastructure migrations, taking themselves offline within hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, citing direct risk to their operations.

Underground operators face a dual threat: both law enforcement and rival criminal groups could weaponize PHP2Shell against forum infrastructure storing member identities, private communications, and stolen credentials.

The adversary response mirrors legitimate enterprise incident response, including emergency patching, platform migration, and business continuity planning.

Historical precedent from the 2024 BreachForums seizure conditioned criminal operators to treat infrastructure vulnerabilities as existential business risks

Background

PHP powers an estimated 75% of websites with identifiable server-side technology, making it the backbone of the modern web. That infrastructure extends far beyond legitimate businesses. Criminal forums, dark web marketplaces, and underground communication platforms rely on the same PHP-based software stacks, such as phpBB, custom forum engines, and web-based administration panels, that power their legitimate counterparts.

On Oct. 20, 2026, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP were publicly disclosed: CVE-2026-109618 (OOM Corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (Stale Global State), each carrying a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. The two flaws target different stages of PHP’s memory management, and chaining them together yields a more reliable exploitation path than either alone. Researchers credit frontier AI models with both the initial discovery and the exploitation chain connecting them. Tenable Vulnerability Watch classified both as Vulnerabilities of Concern (VOC). Within hours, the cybersecurity community began its familiar cycle of assessment, patching, and remediation. (For a full technical breakdown, see our blog “php2shell: Frequently asked questions about critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities”.)

At the same time, a parallel response was already underway including criminal forum self-evacuations and steps to protect the adversary economy.

“We take our security seriously”

The adversary economy operates on the same fundamental principles as the legitimate economy. Criminal operators invest in infrastructure, manage risk, plan for business continuity, and respond to threats against their operations with the same systematic urgency that any well-run organization would apply. From the credential theft supply chains we documented earlier this year to the infrastructure-level emergency playing out now, a consistent pattern emerges: the underground functions as an economy, and economies have attack surfaces. PHP2Shell affected both sides of the security divide simultaneously, and the underground's response demonstrates that sophisticated threat actors have already internalized the severity of this exposure.

Within 48 hours of PHP2Shell disclosure, administrators across multiple major criminal forums posted emergency notices to their communities. BreachForums, one of the largest English-language criminal marketplaces, posted an advisory that included a phrase familiar to anyone who has read a corporate breach notification: “We take our security seriously.”

The irony is difficult to overstate. A platform best known for trafficking stolen credentials, facilitating ransomware operations, and hosting leaked corporate data deployed the same language that Fortune 500 companies use after their own security incidents. But behind the borrowed corporate-speak was genuine operational urgency.

BreachForums was not alone. DarkForums posted its own shutdown notice: “DF will remain offline until PHP has been patched globally.” PwnForums went dark without explanation. Dread, the Reddit-like platform serving the Tor ecosystem, posted a maintenance notice explicitly naming both CVEs. Several forums temporarily restricted new registrations, and others migrated critical communications to Telegram channels as a contingency measure, treating their PHP-based web platforms as potentially compromised infrastructure.

The dual threat

The urgency behind these evacuations reflects a threat model that legitimate organizations would recognize immediately. Criminal forums run on PHP infrastructure, and that infrastructure stores exactly the kind of data that makes a vulnerability like PHP2Shell catastrophic.

The simultaneous self-evacuation is a significant behavioral indicator. Analysis from DarkOwl, a dark web intelligence firm, highlighted the scope of what sits behind a typical forum’s PHP application layer: member email addresses, IP logs, private messages, financial transaction records, and the very stolen credentials that members uploaded for sale. A successful exploit of a forum’s PHP stack would not merely disrupt the platform. It would expose the identities and operational security of every participant.

Forum operators face a threat that most legitimate businesses do not: the adversary attacks from two directions simultaneously. Law enforcement agencies have demonstrated both the capability and the willingness to exploit criminal infrastructure, as the FBI’s operation against Hive ransomware and multiple forum takedowns have shown. But rival criminal groups represent an equally serious threat. Competing forums, extortionists, and opportunistic hackers all have incentive to breach a rival platform’s database to steal its user base, to extort its operators, or to eliminate competition.

This dual threat transforms a PHP vulnerability from a technical issue into an existential business risk. The criminal underground last evacuated platforms at this scale during the 2024 BreachForums seizure — but that response was triggered by law enforcement action. PHP2Shell marks the first time a technical vulnerability in shared infrastructure provoked the same reaction, a shift suggesting criminal operators now treat their PHP dependency as a systemic single point of failure. They evaluate this exposure in precisely the same terms as a CISO assessing a critical unpatched vulnerability: the question is not whether someone will attempt exploitation, but when.

The BreachForums lesson

That institutional memory was shaped by hard experience. The 2024 FBI seizure of BreachForums demonstrated in concrete terms what happens when criminal infrastructure is compromised.

That seizure resulted in the exposure of operational details, the arrest of the forum’s administrator, and the disruption of thousands of active criminal operations that depended on the platform. For the underground economy, it was the equivalent of a major supply chain breach: a single point of failure that cascaded across an entire ecosystem.

The lesson was absorbed. Criminal operators began treating their web infrastructure as a single point of failure requiring the same resilience planning that legitimate enterprises apply to critical systems. PHP2Shell validated that concern. The two CVEs affect every PHP version below 8.3, meaning that the approximately 59% of internet-facing PHP hosts running end-of-life branches are permanently exposed absent a version upgrade. Criminal forums running older PHP versions face the same impossible math as any enterprise with a large install base of unsupported software: the patch does not exist, and the only remediation is migration.

From defense to offense: the exploit economy

The criminal underground’s relationship with PHP2Shell extends beyond defensive measures. Intelligence reporting indicates that exploit code for both CVEs circulated in private channels before the public embargo lifted, with pre-disclosure exploitation observed as early as Oct. 17 from infrastructure traced to an IP address geolocated in Australia.

The exploit development pipeline has accelerated in ways that should concern every organization running PHP. Researchers have documented the use of AI-assisted vulnerability analysis tools to accelerate the development of working exploits and to identify additional exploitation vectors within the disclosed vulnerability classes. This represents a broader trend in which the same AI capabilities that accelerate defensive security research simultaneously compress the window between disclosure and weaponization.

The monetization forecast follows a pattern we have documented before. The developer credential economy operates through three layers (generation, distribution, and weaponization), and PHP2Shell maps cleanly onto each. Initial access brokers will package PHP2Shell exploitation into their service offerings. Ransomware affiliates will incorporate the vulnerabilities into their initial access playbooks. And the criminal forums that patched their own infrastructure will become the marketplaces for selling access to organizations that did not. We saw a preview of this commoditization cycle during the Miasma campaign, where open-sourced attack toolchains accelerated exploitation at scale. The adversary economy is efficient: the same operators who scrambled to protect their own PHP stacks will profit from organizations that fail to do the same.

What this means for defenders

The criminal underground’s reaction to PHP2Shell is, paradoxically, one of the clearest available signals of the vulnerability’s severity. When threat actors treat a disclosure as an emergency requiring immediate operational response, defenders should calibrate their own urgency accordingly.

Organizations running PHP should treat both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as immediate remediation priorities. Every PHP version below 8.3 is affected, and no patches will be issued for end-of-life branches including all of PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, 8.1, and 8.2. For environments where an immediate upgrade is not feasible, compensating controls including web application firewalls, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for exploitation indicators should be deployed without delay. The criminals have already patched. The question for every organization is whether they will do the same before the exploit economy catches up.

Identifying affected systems

Title: How to contain shadow AI, as it takes on multiple forms and spreads throughout your environment
Context: That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data
Full Text:
Shadow AI used to be confined to a few simple scenarios, such as AI chatbots and AI browser extensions. Today, it spans a broad spectrum of complex vectors, making it harder to detect and control. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how employee security training, AI usage governance, and exposure management can help you tackle shadow AI successfully.

Key takeaways

Integrating shadow AI into security awareness training helps employees recognize its risks and learn how to safely adopt AI tools. Security teams should foster open communication with employees and try to understand why they use unsanctioned AI products.

Shadow AI now spans local models, AI coding assistants, autonomous agents, and many other asset types across your environment, making it a pervasive and complex problem.

You can reduce shadow AI incidence by enacting an AI acceptable use policy that provides clear guidelines and a list of approved AI tools, and by addressing shadow AI as part of your unified exposure management program.

It’s an ordinary workday at a typical mid-to-large enterprise, and the following is happening without the knowledge of the IT and security departments:

A marketing manager installs an unvetted, open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to secretly bridge his desktop AI assistant with the company’s internal customer database.

A sales executive downloads a free AI browser extension to summarize a web page, unknowingly granting a third party read-access to her confidential CRM dashboards.

An accounting supervisor creates custom AI chatbot skills to automate his reporting, feeding unredacted financial projections into a public generative AI tool.

An engineer bypasses software restrictions to download and run an unvetted, locally hosted AI model, creating a massive blind spot for endpoint security.

A business analyst hands over her broad administrative credentials to a consumer-grade AI agent so it can autonomously crawl the company’s private data warehouse.

A developer pastes proprietary, unreleased source code into a free, web-based AI assistant for quick debugging, inadvertently surrendering corporate IP to a public model’s training set.

Yes, we’ve come a long way from the days when instances of shadow AI consisted mostly of employees oversharing work information with their personal AI chatbot. With AI now permeating enterprises’ operations, shadow AI has spread and morphed accordingly across the attack surface. It has become riskier and harder to detect, especially as autonomous AI agents proliferate.

For example, security incidents involving organizations’ shadow AI assets have more than doubled to 43%, compared with 20% last year, according to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report.” Meanwhile, the average data breach cost of shadow AI-related incidents hit $5.39 million, about $400,000 above the global average.

IBM's report found a direct impact on data privacy, operations, and compliance:

Almost half of shadow AI security incidents resulted in data loss or data compromise

42% caused operational disruption

21% triggered regulatory fines

During a 30-day period earlier this year, the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform found 457 million security issues across 7,000 customer environments using 274 detection plugins built specifically for AI. That averaged out to about 62,000 AI-related exposures per customer.

“The enterprise AI landscape of 2026 bears little resemblance to the AI landscape of even three years ago,” the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) wrote in its April report, “The Invisible Enterprise: Shadow AI and the Ungoverned Frontier.”

Because AI adoption has “dramatically outpaced” organizations’ AI governance, many enterprises now have a dangerous “invisible layer of AI infrastructure” that hasn’t been inventoried, and thus isn’t subjected to policy enforcement, access controls, or audits, according to the CSA report.

In this third installment of Tenable’s weekly Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, we’ll unpack best practices organizations can adopt to tackle shadow AI in its multiple forms — AI code assistants, models, applications, APIs, embedded features, agents, MCP servers, training data, browser extensions, and more — and mitigate its risks, such as compliance failures, system breaches, and data leaks.

3 steps to help you mitigate the risk from shadow AI

1. Boost employee and leadership awareness and education

A logical place to start your campaign against shadow AI is by teaching employees and leaders how to recognize and prevent the issue.

Employees

Just last month, the U.K. government stressed how important it is for organizations to address the human factor in shadow AI, specifically the disconnect between employees’ fast adoption and organizations’ lag in approving AI tools and setting AI usage policies.

For example, 34% of employees polled in Thomson Reuters’ “Future of Professionals 2026” report admitted to knowingly and deliberately using AI wares their organization hasn’t approved.

Why? “They are frustrated by the quality of sanctioned tools or the lack of a clear AI strategy,” reads a Thomson Reuters article about the report, published in June.

The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends focusing on three key elements:

Understand why staffers use unapproved AI tools.

Establish a “positive cybersecurity culture” marked by open communication between employees and the security team.

Securely integrate AI systems into the workplace.

“By raising awareness of the risks of shadow AI use within your organization and understanding the needs of employees, you can help them get the benefits of new technologies while using them securely,” an NCSC cloud researcher wrote in the blog “The hidden risks of shadow AI.”

In other words, focus on employee education, not punishment, and include shadow AI in your security awareness program training.

Business unit leaders

Proactively reach out to business unit leaders to learn about the AI tools they’re using, their reasons for using them, and the benefits they yield. Engaging in this needs-assessment exercise can help you decide which AI tools to allow and which ones to prohibit.

2. Establish a clear AI governance policy

Avoid being seen as an enemy of AI adoption. Extremely restrictive approaches, such as “block by default” policies, tend to backfire because they drive employees and teams to push their AI usage further underground, especially if these tools boost their productivity.

Instead, you should adopt an AI acceptable use policy that outlines clear rules for who can use AI, which tools they can use, and what data they can input, in a way that doesn’t compromise security and compliance.

Your AI policy should also clarify levels of accountability by outlining the responsibilities of employees, managers, and the AI governance team. For example, it should stress that employees must verify the accuracy of AI-generated content, because each individual is ultimately responsible for the quality of their work.

The comprehensive policy should clearly outline AI usage guardrails, such as rules for data handling, detail the formal process and criteria that the security and IT teams will use for approving and adopting AI tools, and provide a curated list of authorized tools.

It should further help you assess whether you should outright block a discovered shadow AI tool, or whether you can allow it with the appropriate controls.

Some questions to ask:

Does the AI vendor claim ownership of what your users input into its tool?

Does the tool encrypt data in transit and at rest?

What are the vendor’s vulnerability and incident disclosure processes?

Does the product comply with regulations relevant to your organization, like HIPAA?

Does the vendor use your data to train public AI models?

In which geographic region does the vendor house your data?

Which types of industry compliance does the AI vendor adhere to?

Finally, the AI usage policy should be a living document your organization continually revises, as AI technology advances and the organization’s usage evolves.

“Leaders should focus on creating a governance framework that balances innovation with risk management, ensuring employees feel empowered to use GenAI responsibly,” reads Deloitte’s “GenAI Workforce Survey,” which was published in September. The report found that 31% of U.K. employees use AI tools without their organizations’ permission.

3. Address shadow AI as part of your broader exposure management program

With AI now pervasive across most enterprises, shadow AI is present throughout your IT environment in a wide variety of manifestations. This is precisely the type of complex and multidimensional security issue that a unified exposure management platform helps untangle.

At Tenable, we believe that trying to detect and control shadow AI as a standalone problem with isolated point tools is the wrong approach.

To successfully mitigate AI security risks, including shadow AI, you need to gather contextually rich AI security data, so you can correlate and analyze it alongside your other exposure data. That way, you can see how your security issues combine to create attack paths that lead to your most critical systems and data.

These are some key ways in which an exposure management platform can help you address shadow AI risk.

Obtain comprehensive visibility of your AI environment via a continuously updated inventory of your AI assets – what they are, who and what can access them, and which data they can access – wherever they are in your environment including in your:

Data centers

Endpoints

Web apps

Cloud workloads

Network traffic

Application development pipelines

Enterprise AI platforms

Operational technology (OT) systems

IoT infrastructure

Detect shadow AI assets’ security flaws, including vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, excessive permissions, insecure output handling, and exposed training data.

Contextually map and prioritize the security issues that require immediate attention across your entire attack surface based on factors like AI asset criticality and business impact.

Take action and automate remediation, including by leveraging agentic AI capabilities, to carry out the fixes needed to close your shadow AI exposures.

Reduce the risk of data getting shared improperly via AI prompts and uploads by:

Discovering and classifying sensitive data

Auditing AI assets’ permissions and enforcing least-privilege policies

Monitoring data flows in real time

Detecting and blocking sensitive intellectual property, proprietary source code, and customers’ personally identifiable information (PII) before exposure or compromise

Title: How Tenable brought multi-language support to security detectors with agentic translation
Context: AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection
Full Text:
AI security tools that can only detect threats in English offer limited protection. Here’s how Tenable trained our threat detectors to process nine additional languages and understand thousands more, without the need for a translation model, which increases costs and slows down processing.

Key takeaways

Tenable One AI Exposure’s detectors, covering AI threats, harmful content, and other policy risks, were originally English-centric. To assess threats written in other languages, our product translated them into English, a slow, expensive, and often imprecise approach.

Tenable built an agentic translation pipeline that generates high-fidelity, label-preserving training and benchmark data across nine languages, guarded by a multi-judge quality gate, a refinement loop, and a model-refusal handling fallback.

This single multilingual model detects threats natively in all 10 supported languages. Compared with our previous process of translating threats into English, this model is roughly 20-800 times faster per item and is less expensive by an order of magnitude, bearing a one-time cost that does not grow with usage traffic from our customers.

Why your AI security tool should support multiple languages

A prompt attack against an AI model written in Spanish, Arabic, or Hindi is every bit as dangerous as one written in English, which is why an English-only AI security detector will leave your organization at risk from non-English attacks.

To address this issue in our product, Tenable first adopted a “translate-then-detect” process:

Identify the language.

Translate the input to English with a large translation model.

Then run the English detector.

This process works, but it has four downsides:

Latency. A large, autoregressive translation model that runs before every non-English detection needs hundreds of milliseconds for short inputs, and seconds to tens of seconds for long ones.

Cost. Every non-English request pays for a full translation pass.

Operational overhead. You have to serve, scale, and maintain another heavyweight model.

Lost signal. Meaning and intent blur in naive translation, which degrades the tool’s ability to detect threats.

How Tenable turned our AI security tool into a polyglot

To make our AI security product natively multilingual, we discovered that we didn’t need to use a translator LLM in production. Instead, we found that we needed high-quality multilingual data in two places:

A training set to teach the model the target languages.

A test set we could trust to benchmark performance honestly in each language.

Both must preserve the labels of the data, ensuring that the label survives the translation process. Translation can quietly flip a label (a malicious data sample rendered as a benign one) or defang it (the security-relevant language “bite” softened so that what’s a clear positive in the original language instead reads as a borderline threat). Either way, the data sample is now mislabeled and poisons the data.

Tenable concluded that the following methods are not ideal:

Human-expert translation. It is slow and needs a fluent reviewer for every language, so it does not scale.

Machine translation. Standard translation methods distort dataset quality in two distinct ways: native machine translation prioritizes smooth phrasing over security context, potentially stripping out malicious intent (e.g., turning a toxin synthesis request into a benign chemistry query), while direct, word-for-word translation creates awkward, unnaturally phrased text that degrades training signal, such as an English phishing lure translated literally into Japanese.

Off-the-shelf LLMs. They may refuse to translate material they flag as inappropriate, such as prompts about weapons synthesis or self-harm topics, so the text that represents a likely threat gets left out of the dataset.

Always-on (online) translators. Relying on online translation pipelines introduces per-request latency, operational complexity, and costs that scale with hundreds of millions of items, making it impractical for production environments.

The translation process has to be cost-effective and repeatable across many languages.

The Tenable solution: An agentic pipeline plus a multilingual model

1. The agentic pipeline overview

The agentic translation pipeline. Each English item is transcreated by a frontier LLM, scored by a panel of independent judges, and either accepted or sent back to refine. On a refusal, a controlled open-source model takes over, via the same gate.

In Tenable’s data translation process, every item flows through three stages in our agentic pipeline.

Translate. A frontier LLM produces a transcreation, a translation that we fine-tune by specifying the task, the item’s label, and the target language, as opposed to a blind word-for-word rendering. This fine-tuning is precisely what keeps the security-relevant meaning, and the label, intact.

Estimate. A panel of independent judges scores each translation for fluency, meaning integrity, and whether the original data label still holds.

Gate. Only translations that clear every check are kept.

Two recovery loops keep the hard cases from being lost:

Refusal handling. When the frontier translator refuses a sensitive item, the pipeline hands the same transcreation job to a controlled, open-source small-language model that does not refuse, and its output goes through the same quality gate, so legitimate-but-sensitive security data is not silently dropped.

Refinement. When a translation fails the quality gate, it is sent back for another attempt rather than thrown away.

Because the task and labels are parameters, the pipeline can serve any future detection task requiring multilingual support.

2. A pretrained multilingual model

Instead of training a language model from scratch, we fine-tuned a compact model that was already pretrained on many languages, which yielded two benefits:

It consumes far less data per language. The model has already learned useful cross-lingual representations, so we only taught it our task.

It transfers knowledge between languages. We measured this before spending a dollar on translation. For some tasks, the model successfully generalized to other languages using only English training data, eliminating the need for translation. For harder tasks, we used the agentic translation framework to translate only to the languages in which the model underperformed. Even in those cases, training the model on a handful of languages lifted the model’s translation performance in other languages at no additional cost.

Impact and results

By replacing our legacy translate-then-detect architecture with a single native model, Tenable transformed our pipeline into an enterprise-grade solution that delivers near-instantaneous global coverage. This shift drastically reduced latency and infrastructure costs while maintaining top-tier quality and unlocking broader language support. Below are the key results achieved by this upgraded architecture:

One fast model, no translator in the path. Detection now runs natively in every supported language in tens of milliseconds, whereas it took seconds with the translate-then-detect process, roughly 20-800× faster per item. In addition, the memory footprint is about 12-14× smaller: under 1 GB versus 12-14 GB.

A one-time cost, under $10,000. We generated the multilingual training and benchmark data once. That cost does not grow with client’s production traffic, unlike an always-on translator, whose bill scales with every request.

Budget-tunable by design. We set the budget, and the pipeline adjusts the tier of LLM it uses and how much refinement each item receives.

Quality you can prove. A neutral LLM-as-a-judge from a third-party model family, outside our translation and grading stack, preferred Tenable transcreations over those from a commercial machine translation model and over those from a strong open translation model in the large majority of head-to-head comparisons.

No English regression. Every Tenable One AI Exposure detector gained the ability to understand and translate from nine languages (Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, and Hindi) while English performance held or improved, and latency stayed near real-time.

Reach beyond the languages we trained. Because the model was pretrained on a very broad set of languages, the same model can read and flag attacks in thousands of languages we never explicitly trained it on. We have only formally validated the 10 languages we support, so this wider reach is promising but needs further testing before it can be relied on.

AI-threat detection, recall @ 0.005% false positive rate. (The recall metric measures how good a system is at finding every single relevant item without missing any.) Our multilingual model matches or beats translate-then-detect on 9 of 10 languages and overall (0.93 vs 0.88).

Harmful-content detection, recall @ 0.02% false positive rate. On the harder task, the gap widens: our multilingual model leads on every language and overall (0.65 vs 0.50).

How Tenable One AI Exposure protects multilingual users

Threat actors do not limit themselves to English, and neither should your defenses. With this work, Tenable One AI Exposure extends the same detection quality (for jailbreaks, prompt injection, harmful content, and data exposure) natively across 10 languages, at production speed and without a translation bottleneck in the request path. As customers adopt AI in more markets and more languages, that multilingual coverage extends with them.

Full Text:
Discover how to secure AI agents in your cloud environment with Tenable One Cloud Exposure. We explore Microsoft Entra Agent ID and provide essential best practices for robust agentic AI identity security.

Key takeaways

Understand your current maturity level and then build an appropriate action plan to secure your agent identities.

Use your cloud providers’ native tools or Tenable One Cloud Exposure to locate and catalog every AI agent operating in your environment.

Do not assign human identities or over-privileged service accounts to the AI agents your vendors deploy in your environment. Instead, require that vendors adopt official models like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for their AI agents’ identities.

As AI agents move from experimental toys to tools that make autonomous decisions, interact with databases, and call external APIs, organizations need to be clear on who — or what — is executing these actions in their cloud environments.

Why non-human identities (NHIs) aren’t secure enough for AI agents

Security teams categorize identities into two buckets: human identities and non-human identities (NHIs), such as service accounts, secrets, and automated scripts.

Treating AI agents as standard NHIs is a recipe for disaster. AI agents combine their non-deterministic nature with their ability to execute flexible, outcome-oriented actions, rather than following strict, prescribed instructions.

Unlike classic, predictable scripts that follow rigid code paths, AI agents:

Make creative, runtime decisions using LLMs.

Interact with dynamic external tools, memory caches, and knowledge bases.

Constantly adapt to solve problems, making it difficult for a security team to establish AI agents’ baseline behavior.

To address this challenge, major cloud providers have introduced dedicated, specialized agentic AI identity models. Let’s break down one major model: Microsoft Entra Agent ID.

Announcing Tenable One Cloud Exposure support for Microsoft Entra Agent ID

Identity and cloud providers' native identity management tools present only basic information about agentic identities, without providing context about their security flaws and how they extend your attack surface. Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them. At Tenable, we believe visibility is the foundation of security. You can’t secure assets that you do not know exist.

As organization-wide adoption of agentic AI accelerates, the immediate challenge for security teams is first and foremost finding them. Because these identities are brand new, conventional identity and access management (IAM) systems may not recognize or monitor them, which creates security blind spots.

To help our customers address this issue, Tenable One Cloud Exposure now brings Microsoft Entra agentic AI identities directly into your unified asset and identity inventory.

Microsoft Entra Agent ID Model

The Microsoft Entra Agent ID framework functions through a four-tiered structural model:

Agent identity blueprints serve as the master templates for shared attributes. Residing exclusively within the agent provider’s home tenant, they establish cross-tenant links that heighten exposure to potential supply-chain attacks.

Agent identity blueprint principals are the localized instantiation of a blueprint within every specific tenant where the AI agent is deployed and active.

Agent identities represent the functional identities utilized for routine tasks. To maintain oversight of agent behavior, these are the primary entities your security team must monitor.

Agent users offer an optional layer for each agent identity requiring human-centric features — like Microsoft Teams access or a personal mailbox — to function effectively as integrated “digital colleagues.”
